title: Equivalent clean price
summary: Compare whether buying the product as purchased (with trim) or already clean is cheaper.

what: Many raw materials can be bought untrimmed (with trim) or trimmed. The trimmed price is always higher, because the supplier absorbs the trim and the labor of cleaning.
You can't compare an untrimmed price with a trimmed one directly: first work out your own equivalent clean price.
formula: Equivalent clean price = as-purchased price × waste factor

variables.name: As-purchased price
variables.description: What you pay per kilo for the product as it comes.

variables.name: Waste factor
variables.description: Comes from the trim waste % of that product.

variables.name: Equivalent clean price
variables.description: What each clean kilo really costs you if you buy it untrimmed.

steps: Find out the trim waste % of the product.
Multiply the as-purchased price by the factor.
Compare it with the supplier's clean price.
Before deciding, weigh other factors: whether you have staff to clean it, urgency and storage space.

examples.title: Whole vs. trimmed tenderloin (illustrative)
paragraphs: The handbook leaves this exercise to be completed in class. With sample numbers: whole tenderloin at $10,000 per kilo with 30% trim, and trimmed tenderloin at $15,000 per kilo.
Factor = 1.429. Equivalent clean price = $10,000 × 1.429 = $14,285.71 per kilo.
The supplier's trimmed tenderloin costs $15,000: on price alone, buying it whole and cleaning it yourself is cheaper ($714.29 less per kilo), as long as you have the time and staff.

notes.text: The same comparison works between two suppliers of the same product with different trim: cured ham, squid, eggplants, oranges…
The cheapest isn't always the best buy: the handbook recommends the most convenient one, also considering quality and supplier reliability.
